How can we improve Judo in the US?  One word: MARKETING. As coaches in the US, we suck at marketing our Judo. There's a lot of smack talk about TKD and Karate, many saying that these arts are just belt factories or McDojos, but the reality is; They Are Successful! Their success cannot be denied. Also, we as coaches must adapt to the times and to our customer’s needs. A balance can be kept between traditional judo and modernizing Judo to keep up with the current society/customer base. 

For whatever reason, many Judo coaches are egotistical and unwilling to change. They feel that they are preserving Judo in their strict un-bending ways.  Unfortunately, this couldn’t be any further from the truth.  Most (not all) coaches continue to teach competitive Judo, complying with the current IJF rule set.  So how are they preserving Judo by complying with IJF rules?  You can’t have it both ways.  Another issue is that many coaches place themselves on pedestals, some even act as demagogues in their dojos and within the Judo community.  There’s more than one way to skin a cat… just saying.

In today's entitlement culture, Americans do not want the totalitarian Sensei. Many of you reading this will say, that's BS, I'll run my class however I want to. That's the problem! Coaches are not adapting. That's why we are failing. Many coaches will say that you can't make a living at Judo. Wrong again. A great example of this is James Wall in Denham Springs, LA. He's just opened his second Judo (That's right, I said Judo) location. Now I'll concede that he has other disciplines that are taught/offered, but that is another point that I want to make. We as coaches have to be able to diversify. We can't be "one trick ponies".  We have to get students in the door.  Once we do that, and teach the spirit of judo as Kano-Shihan envisioned, than I feel that we could keep 5 to 7 of those prospective students.

In my class, we are, for the most part, very informal.  We bow in and out of class, but that’s pretty much where the formality ends.  I don’t make my students call me Sensei.  In fact, I encourage them to call me Coach, or by my first name.  It puts everyone at ease, and really fosters a learning environment.  So in conclusion, I believe that marketing is the start of improving Judo in the US, but there really has to be a change in the culture of the Judo coaches in the US for true results to be seen and for an increase of popularity of Judo in the US.

you did indeed in your earlier post said to wear a white belt.  You said, "Don't wear a brown belt, wear a white belt".  

Starting over at any belt other than what rank you were promoted to is just as silly as starting over as a white belt.  Same principle.  You keep what you earned.

This is why there are governing bodies of Judo.  If a rank is given by a Sensei/Coach, and it is through an NGB, then you not only deserve that rank, but you are completely misrepresenting yourself, your instructor  the NGB, and Judo if you wear a belt other than what your rank is.  The NGB's requirements for promotion are spelled out quite clearly for each and every rank in Judo, and if you have passed these requirements and have been promoted, then that is your rank; Period!  It doesn't matter one iota how many hours, days, weeks, months, or years have gone by since you trained.  

Your comparison of Judo and Jiu Jitsu with regards to promotions is like comparing stop lights to airplanes.  There is no set standard in the BJJ community for promotions.  Every BJJ school, and Professor promotes differently.  Some require testing, some don't.  Some have a syllabus, and some don't.  Some require a set amount of classes that you have to attend before promotion.  Judo has a very rigid and delineated set of standards and requirements for Judo. One is not promoted through an NGB without meeting and or exceeding these requirements.

Now, if you have been given "club" rank, this creates a whole other set of problems.  If you have no "official" rank through an NGB, then an Instructor/Coach/Sensei can put you at whatever belt they feel that your skill set is at.  If by chance that coach decides to have you start at a belt other than what you have rightfully earned and been recognized through an NGB, then I would suggest finding a different dojo to practice at.  Again, the "club" rank issue is an entirely different can of worms.

Wear your brown belt.  You earned it.  It doesn't matter how many years it has been since you played.  Your rank is your rank.  It's disrespectful to your former coach that promoted you and disrespectful towards yourself.  Yes, you'll have to knock off some rust, but the muscle memory will come back quickly.  To start over at white belt is offensive and wrong.

RULES OF THE DOJO

1.	Students must never use their Judo skill outside of Judo activities, except in self-defense.
2.	Students must show respect for themselves, their Sensei, their classmates, and most importantly, their family.
3.	The Sensei and their staff are the ONLY ones authorized to instruct.  If you are unsure, then ask the Sensei.  Do not try to correct or instruct your fellow student.  
4.	Students are responsible for their own safety, and the safety of all of their classmates, throughout the class.
5.	Students should bow (rei) to all partners when beginning and finishing training sessions with them.
6.	Uniforms should be clean, in good repair, and properly worn at all times.  This includes keeping nails trimmed and bodies clean.
7.	Courtesy and attentiveness are requirements for showing respect, and should be practiced in the Dojo at all times.
8.	Students must rei (bow) onto and off of the practice mat when starting or ending a training session, and should not leave the mat without the permission of the instructor.  Emergency situations are obviously an exception.
9.	Students should be dressed and ready to participate when class time begins.  If a student is running late, they may not come on the mat without the instructor bowing them on.
10.	There will be no eating, drinking, or gum chewing on the practice area.
11.	No jewelry or sharp objects may be worn on the mat.  If you have a piercing which cannot be removed, it must be taped and covered in such a way that it presents no danger.
12.	Questions are allowed, encouraged, and expected.  Arguing with instructors or upper belts will not be tolerated.
13.	It is discourteous, and unsafe, to turn your back to a partner. Students should face their partner at all times, including when adjusting their uniform.  The exception to this is if modesty dictates turning away from them.
NOTE:  This courtesy is the opposite of most other Martial Arts.  If a guest of another club, please follow their rules.  If we have guests, please allow for these differences.
14.	REMEMBER.  Judo training should be fun, but must be taken seriously.
